questions.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-4y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-4({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
-{b}_{n}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)=\frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{2}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+4)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}+49y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that the free term and all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+49({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain 

$$
{a}_{n}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})=\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}}\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}.
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{2\pi }{{n}^{2}(49-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2})}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{9{\pi }^{2}}=3\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $2$-periodic function $(L=1)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{1}=n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=3\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))+x(-3\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+3\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+9{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x):$

$$
[-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)-9{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+9{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6\pi A=0 \\ 6\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{54\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{54\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi x).
$$

Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x),$ where the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\pi A=4 \\ \pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{4}{\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=-\frac{4x}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}):$

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A=-\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=\frac{9}{16\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{9x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$
